claims.text: Thermal-expansion mismatch between the HfNbTaTiZr matrix and coherent nanoprecipitates or phase boundaries generates internal residual stresses during cooling and thermal cycling.
The mismatch-induced residual stresses modulate dislocation dynamics.
A single residual-stress mechanism explains the alloy's high-temperature creep, cold-rolling microhardness changes, elastic-modulus variations, and aging-induced hardening.
The proposed initial state can be produced by vacuum arc melting, HIP near 1200 °C, and prolonged annealing.
The processed HfNbTaTiZr alloy will have a uniform FCC or BCC matrix with the potential to form coherent nanoprecipitates.
Slow cooling minimizes residual thermal stress, whereas rapid quenching or thermal cycling maximizes mismatch-induced residual stress.
Coherent nanoprecipitates or phase boundaries in HfNbTaTiZr have thermal-expansion coefficients different from that of the primary matrix.
Differential thermal contraction of the matrix and precipitates produces internal residual stresses.
Internal residual stress changes stacking-fault energy and thereby alters dislocation mobility.
Internal residual stress changes dislocation-pinning conditions.
Internal residual stress influences phase stability.
Rapidly quenched or thermally cycled samples will have higher yield strength than slow-cooled samples.
Rapidly quenched or thermally cycled samples will have greater high-temperature creep resistance than slow-cooled samples.
Rapidly quenched or thermally cycled samples will have altered elastic moduli relative to slow-cooled samples.
Aging at 600–800 °C will accentuate treatment-dependent property differences because nanoprecipitate evolution reinforces internal stress fields.
Residual-stress effects will be most measurable above approximately 600 °C.
Residual-stress effects should influence elastic-modulus measurements between 293 and 1100 K but be minimal below room temperature.
Observations in similar alloy systems qualitatively support a role for matrix–precipitate mismatch in mechanical behavior.
The quantitative contribution of residual stress to creep rate, microhardness, and elastic modulus is uncertain.

The hypothesis is falsified if rapid-quench or thermally cycled samples show no statistically significant differences from slow-cooled samples in residual stress or the specified mechanical and thermoelastic responses.
